title: Events in the last 24 hours
scenario: The overnight shift wants to know how much traffic came in since this time yesterday.
task: Return a single count named recent_events for events whose Time falls within the last 24 hours.
hints: Time is epoch milliseconds, so you must either convert the column or convert your boundary.
Converting the boundary is far better: it keeps the column bare so the index can be used.
The boundary in milliseconds is extract(epoch from now() - interval '24 hours') * 1000.
WHERE "Time" >= extract(epoch FROM now() - interval '24 hours') * 1000.

explanation.breakdown: The comparison boundary is computed once as a millisecond epoch, then compared directly against the raw column.
explanation.why: Wrapping the column in to_timestamp() would work but makes the expression non-sargable — the index on Time becomes unusable and every row must be converted.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting the * 1000 and comparing milliseconds against seconds. The boundary lands in 1970, every row qualifies, and the count silently equals the whole table.
explanation.performance: Keep the indexed column bare on one side of the comparison. This is the single most valuable performance habit for time-series filtering.
explanation.qaRelevance: Rolling-window counts are the foundation of every monitoring alert. Getting the unit conversion right once and reusing it prevents a whole family of bugs.

title: Daily event volume
scenario: You want the daily trend line for the last week to see whether volume is stable.
task: Return the event date as day and the count as n for the last 7 days, sorted by day.
expected: Seven or eight rows showing daily totals.
hints: Grouping by day means collapsing each timestamp to midnight of its day.
date_trunc('day', ts) does exactly that.
Convert first: to_timestamp("Time"/1000), then truncate.
Filter with a millisecond boundary in WHERE, and GROUP BY the truncated date.
solution:
SELECT date_trunc('day', to_timestamp("Time" / 1000))::date AS day,
       count(*)                                            AS n
FROM "Events"
WHERE "Time" >= extract(epoch FROM now() - interval '7 days') * 1000
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY day;

explanation.breakdown: date_trunc rounds a timestamp down to the requested precision. Casting to ::date drops the time part entirely, which makes the output cleaner.
explanation.why: The WHERE clause still filters on the raw bigint so the index remains usable; only the surviving rows are converted for grouping.
explanation.commonMistake: Filtering on the converted expression as well, which discards the index and scans everything.
explanation.alternative: date_trunc('week', ...) or ('month', ...) for coarser trends — same shape, different argument.
explanation.qaRelevance: A daily series is the first thing to look at when someone reports 'events dropped'. It immediately tells you whether the change is gradual or a cliff.

title: Yesterday versus the day before
scenario: Operations reports fewer events yesterday. Before investigating cameras, confirm the overall change.
task: Return one row with day_before and yesterday as counts, and the difference (yesterday minus day_before) as delta.
expected: Two totals and a negative delta.
hints: Both numbers come from the same table over two adjacent date ranges — one pass with two filtered aggregates.
The date of an event is to_timestamp("Time"/1000)::date.
Yesterday is CURRENT_DATE - 1; the day before is CURRENT_DATE - 2.
count(*) FILTER (WHERE ... = CURRENT_DATE - 2) and the same for - 1, then subtract.
solution:
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp("Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 2) AS day_before,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp("Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 1) AS yesterday,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp("Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 1)
  - count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp("Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 2) AS delta
FROM "Events"
WHERE "Time" >= extract(epoch FROM CURRENT_DATE - 2) * 1000
  AND "Time" <  extract(epoch FROM CURRENT_DATE)     * 1000;

explanation.breakdown: The outer WHERE narrows to the two days of interest so the scan stays small; the FILTER clauses then split those rows into the two buckets.
explanation.why: Note the half-open range: >= start AND < end. Using <= CURRENT_DATE would include today's partial data and make the comparison misleading.
explanation.commonMistake: Comparing a full day against a partial day. It is the most common reason a 'drop' turns out to be an artefact of when the query ran.
explanation.alternative: A grouped query with LAG() computes day-over-day deltas for every day at once — see Level 7.
explanation.qaRelevance: Always confirm the aggregate change is real before drilling into individual devices. Half of reported 'drops' are boundary errors in the report itself.

title: Which camera dropped the most yesterday
scenario: Total volume is down. Now find which camera is responsible.
task: For each camera return Name as camera, its day-before count as day_before, its yesterday count as yesterday, and the difference as delta. Show only cameras where delta is negative. Sort by delta ascending then camera.
expected: The cameras that fell, worst first. ANPR-Gate-01 leads by a wide margin.
hints: Same two-bucket idea as before, but grouped per camera.
Join to VideoSources so the output names the camera.
The negative-delta test involves aggregates, so it belongs in HAVING.
HAVING count(*) FILTER (yesterday) - count(*) FILTER (day_before) < 0.
solution:
SELECT v."Name" AS camera,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 2) AS day_before,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 1) AS yesterday,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 1)
       - count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 2) AS delta
FROM "Events" e
JOIN "VideoSources" v ON v."Id" = e."VideoSourceId"
WHERE e."Time" >= extract(epoch FROM CURRENT_DATE - 2) * 1000
  AND e."Time" <  extract(epoch FROM CURRENT_DATE)     * 1000
GROUP BY v."Name"
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 1)
     - count(*) FILTER (WHERE to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)::date = CURRENT_DATE - 2) < 0
ORDER BY delta ASC, camera;

explanation.breakdown: Per-camera two-bucket comparison. HAVING repeats the expression because an output alias is not visible to HAVING.
explanation.why: A camera that produced nothing on both days never appears — it forms no group. A camera that died before the window is invisible to this query entirely, which is why the silent-camera check is separate.
explanation.commonMistake: Assuming the biggest absolute drop is the biggest problem. A camera falling from 40 to 6 matters far more proportionally than one falling from 900 to 880.
explanation.alternative: Compute the percentage change as well, to rank by proportion rather than absolute volume.
explanation.qaRelevance: This is step two of the standard drop investigation: confirm the total, then attribute it to devices.

title: Find the hours with no events at all
scenario: A gap in the data is invisible in a GROUP BY, because a missing hour simply produces no row. You need to see the holes.
task: For camera 'PERIM-North-07' over the last 5 days, return every hour as hour_slot and the event count as n, including hours with zero events. Sort by hour_slot.
expected: 120 hourly rows, nearly all with n = 0 because this camera stopped reporting.
hints: A GROUP BY can only produce rows for data that exists. To show absent hours you must generate them.
generate_series(start, stop, interval '1 hour') produces a row per hour.
LEFT JOIN the generated series to the aggregated events, so hours with no match survive.
Wrap the count in COALESCE(..., 0), or count a column from the right-hand side so unmatched hours count zero.
solution:
WITH slots AS (
  SELECT generate_series(
           date_trunc('hour', now()) - interval '5 days',
           date_trunc('hour', now()),
           interval '1 hour') AS hour_slot
),
hits AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('hour', to_timestamp(e."Time"/1000)) AS hour_slot,
         count(*) AS n
  FROM "Events" e
  JOIN "VideoSources" v ON v."Id" = e."VideoSourceId"
  WHERE v."Name" = 'PERIM-North-07'
    AND e."Time" >= extract(epoch FROM now() - interval '5 days') * 1000
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT s.hour_slot,
       COALESCE(h.n, 0) AS n
FROM slots s
LEFT JOIN hits h ON h.hour_slot = s.hour_slot
ORDER BY s.hour_slot;

explanation.breakdown: generate_series manufactures the complete set of hour slots. The real data is aggregated separately, then LEFT JOINed onto that skeleton so every slot appears.
explanation.why: Absence of data produces absence of rows. Any monitoring query built purely on GROUP BY is blind to outages by construction.
explanation.commonMistake: Reporting 'no anomalies' because the grouped result looked continuous. It looked continuous because the gaps were not rows.
explanation.alternative: In Level 7, LAG() over the actual events finds unusually large gaps without generating a full calendar — cheaper for sparse checks.
explanation.performance: generate_series is cheap; the cost is the aggregation. Bound the range tightly.
explanation.qaRelevance: This is the query that proves a camera went dark and, crucially, exactly when. That timestamp is what you correlate against deployment and network logs.

title: The most recent event overall
scenario: You want a quick liveness check: when did the system last record anything?
task: Return the latest event time as a timestamp named last_event_at, and how many whole minutes ago that was as minutes_ago.
expected: One row. Note that future-dated events make this later than now.
hints: max("Time") gives the largest epoch value; convert it for display.
to_timestamp(max("Time")/1000) turns it into a timestamp.
Subtracting that from now() gives an interval.
extract(epoch from interval)/60 converts an interval to minutes.

explanation.breakdown: max() finds the extreme value; the conversion and arithmetic are applied to that single result.
explanation.why: The answer is negative, because this dataset contains future-dated events. A liveness check that trusts max() would report the system as healthy even if it had stopped hours ago.
explanation.commonMistake: Using max("Time") as a liveness signal without excluding future timestamps. A single bad clock makes the check permanently green.
explanation.alternative: max("Time") FILTER (WHERE "Time" <= extract(epoch from now())*1000) ignores impossible values.
explanation.qaRelevance: Monitoring built on max(timestamp) fails silently when one device has a wrong clock. Always bound the maximum at the present moment.

title: Events straddling the reporting boundary
scenario: Yesterday's report and today's dashboard disagree. One possibility: events that happened yesterday but arrived today, counted differently depending on which timestamp the report uses.
task: Count events where Time falls on yesterday but ReceivedTime falls on today or later. Return one column named late_arrivals.
expected: The events whose occurrence day and arrival day differ across the midnight boundary.
hints: Two independent date conditions, one on each timestamp column.
Convert each with to_timestamp(col/1000)::date.
Time must equal CURRENT_DATE - 1; ReceivedTime must be CURRENT_DATE or later.
Both conditions in the same WHERE, joined with AND.
solution:
SELECT count(*) AS late_arrivals
FROM "Events"
WHERE to_timestamp("Time"/1000)::date         = CURRENT_DATE - 1
  AND to_timestamp("ReceivedTime"/1000)::date >= CURRENT_DATE;

explanation.breakdown: The two columns are filtered independently, isolating rows where the event day and the arrival day disagree.
explanation.why: A report grouped by Time and a dashboard grouped by ReceivedTime will disagree by exactly this set of rows. Neither is wrong — they answer different questions.
explanation.commonMistake: Assuming the two timestamps are interchangeable. Choosing between 'when it happened' and 'when we learned about it' is a product decision that must be stated in the report.
explanation.alternative: Comparing date_trunc('day', ...) of both columns finds all mismatches, not only forward ones — including the clock-skewed camera whose events arrive before they happen.
explanation.qaRelevance: This is the root cause behind a large share of 'the numbers do not match' tickets. Establishing which timestamp each report uses usually resolves the argument in minutes.

title: Weekly volume per event type
scenario: Product wants a weekly trend by analytic type to see which features are growing.
task: Return the week start as week, the EventName as event_name, and the count as n, for the four highest-volume event names only. Sort by week then event_name.
expected: A grid of weeks by event type.
hints: Truncate to week with date_trunc('week', ...), which returns the Monday of that week.
You need to restrict to the top four event names, which is itself an aggregate question.
Use a subquery in WHERE: "EventName" IN (SELECT ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 4).
Group the outer query by both week and event name.
solution:
SELECT date_trunc('week', to_timestamp("Time"/1000))::date AS week,
       "EventName"                                        AS event_name,
       count(*)                                           AS n
FROM "Events"
WHERE "EventName" IN (
  SELECT "EventName" FROM "Events"
  GROUP BY "EventName"
  ORDER BY count(*) DESC
  LIMIT 4
)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY week, event_name;

explanation.breakdown: The IN subquery is evaluated once to produce the four names; the outer query then groups the filtered rows by week and name.
explanation.why: date_trunc('week', ...) anchors weeks on Monday in PostgreSQL. If your business week starts on Sunday you must offset, and getting this wrong shifts every number by a day.
explanation.commonMistake: Assuming weeks start on Sunday, or comparing week numbers across systems that use different conventions.
explanation.alternative: A window function ranking event names by volume avoids the second scan of Events.
explanation.performance: The subquery scans the whole table once. On a large table, restrict its time range too.
explanation.qaRelevance: Weekly aggregation smooths daily noise and makes genuine trend breaks visible — the right granularity for release-over-release comparison.

title: Last seen, per camera
scenario: You want a fleet liveness table: when did each camera last report, and is that acceptable?
task: For every camera return Name as camera, the last event timestamp as last_seen, hours since then as hours_since, and a status of 'SILENT' when more than 48 hours or never, else 'ALIVE'. Include cameras with no events. Sort by camera.
expected: All 42 cameras, with the silent one and the two never-reporting ones flagged.
hints: Start from VideoSources and LEFT JOIN Events so cameras with none survive.
max(e."Time") over the group is NULL for a camera with no events.
Converting NULL yields NULL, so the CASE must test for NULL explicitly before comparing hours.
Group by the camera name, and remember aggregates ignore NULLs.
solution:
SELECT v."Name" AS camera,
       to_timestamp(max(e."Time") / 1000) AS last_seen,
       floor(extract(epoch FROM now() - to_timestamp(max(e."Time")/1000)) / 3600)::int AS hours_since,
       CASE
         WHEN max(e."Time") IS NULL THEN 'SILENT'
         WHEN now() - to_timestamp(max(e."Time")/1000) > interval '48 hours' THEN 'SILENT'
         ELSE 'ALIVE'
       END AS status
FROM "VideoSources" v
LEFT JOIN "Events" e ON e."VideoSourceId" = v."Id"
GROUP BY v."Name"
ORDER BY camera;

explanation.breakdown: LEFT JOIN keeps every camera; max() over an empty set returns NULL rather than erroring; the CASE handles that NULL first.
explanation.why: Two different situations produce a SILENT verdict — a camera that stopped and a camera that never started. Both need attention, and the NULL branch is what makes the second one visible.
explanation.commonMistake: Using an inner join, which drops exactly the cameras you most need to see.
explanation.alternative: A correlated scalar subquery per camera reads more clearly to some, at similar cost here.
explanation.performance: One aggregate over the whole Events table. A production version should restrict to a recent window.
explanation.qaRelevance: This is the single most useful operational query in the whole course: one row per device, one column that says whether to worry.
